In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

insulin increases glucose uptake by the heart and stimulates its metabolism, but that the effect of insulin on the metabolism of glucose by the heart is different from the effect of insulin in other tissues and different from the effect on the metabolism of the heart of an increased glucose concentration in the perfusion medium.

the effect of insulin on the metabolism of the isolated working heart is to stimulate glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and (14)Co(2) production, whereas the effect of a work-load is to stimulate (14)C(2) production and glycolysis, and to decrease glycogen synthesis.

the effects of insulin are to enhance the oxidation of glucose to CO(2) by the heart, to stimulate the formation of glycogen and to stimulate the formation from glucose of the tricarboxylate cycle intermediates which are utilized as fuel by the heart.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insulin increases glucose uptake and oxidation in the heart, but does not increase glucose phosphorylation or glycolysis.
insulin stimulates glucose metabolism by increasing the rate of glucose transport across the cell membrane.

in the perfused rat heart, glucose metabolism in the presence of a work load is stimulated by insulin, but the mechanism of the action of insulin is not simply that of increasing the concentration of glucose available to the heart muscle cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
insulin has an important role in the regulation of glucose metabolism in working hearts.
the metabolic pattern in the heart is more complex than previously thought.
the metabolic pattern of glucose in the heart is more complex than the pattern in diaphragm.
